https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Vessels in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on 3 August 2026 Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen Vessels in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on 3 August 2026 Photograph: Reuters Strait of Hormuz Iran and Oman reach understanding on coordinates of route through Hormuz, Iran ministry says Joint statement is being finalised, but Tehran says deal alone would not guarantee waterway’s security Middle East crisis live – latest updates Reuters Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.03 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Iran and Oman have reached an understanding on ⁠the geographic coordinates for a shipping route through the strait of Hormuz, and ⁠a joint announcement ⁠is ​being finalised, provided certain third parties did not interfere, Iran ’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil ⁠Baghaei said on Wednesday. Baghaei added that any such agreement between Iran and Oman would not, by ⁠itself, guarantee security in the strategic waterway. The proposed deal between ​Iran and Oman would ‌give Tehran control ‌over ships entering the gulf through the strait of Hormuz, ‌a senior Iranian source and two regional officials told Reuters on Wednesday, in one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran . Despite the apparent step towards yielding to Iranian demands, the sources pushed back against assertions ‌by Donald Trump that a deal reopening the strait was imminent, saying important details ​still had to be agreed. Baghaei described the negotiations between Tehran and Muscat as “professional” and “moving forward”, saying “the two sides had reached a mutual understanding ⁠on the geographical parameters of the route under discussion.” Baghaei ​added ​that, if some third ​parties do not obstruct the process, the joint ​statement between ‌the two ​countries, containing the ​main considerations and key points of understanding, was in the final stages of review and drafting. https://www.dw.com/en/several-injured-af.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O76U Major airlines have suspended operations in Riyadh amid security threats [FILE: February 15, 2023] Image: Markus Mainka/picture alliance Advertisement A number of people were injured in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh on Saturday, the country's civil aviation authority has confirmed. A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal. The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity. "ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh." Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport. The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity." Strikes hit Riyadh Airport earlier this week The reports come amid intensified fighting between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen. The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes. Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their ​respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday. King Khalid Airport was hit earlier this week in an attack claimed by Yemen-based Houthi rebels Image: Social Media/REUTERS There was no immediate Houthi statement about the reported blast on Saturday. Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains. The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July. The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait.
